t: Minimum Split Into Subarrays With GCD Greater Than One
o: Partition the array into contiguous pieces, each having GCD > 1, minimizing the piece count. In [12,6,3,14,8] the split [12,6,3],[14,8] costs 2 because the whole array has GCD 1. Key facts: extending a segment can only decrease (or keep) its GCD, and GCD becomes 1 permanently once it hits 1. This monotonicity enables both an O(n²) DP and a greedy that extends each segment as far as possible.
k: GCD of a growing segment is non-increasing; once it reaches 1 it can never recover.
Greedy maximal extension is optimal: pushing a boundary later never hurts later segments.

a.n: Approach 1: Interval DP with backward GCD
a.i: dp[i] = minimum pieces covering the first i elements. For each i, walk j backward maintaining the running GCD of nums[j..i]; while the GCD exceeds 1, dp[i] can be dp[j-1] + 1. Stop as soon as the GCD hits 1 since longer segments are invalid.
s: For each end i, extend start j leftward accumulating gcd; while gcd > 1 relax dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[j-1] + 1).
Break the inner loop when gcd becomes 1.
a.t: O(n² log V) — for each end, the inner walk runs until the GCD dies; worst case quadratic

a.i: Because GCD only shrinks as a segment grows, making each segment as long as possible never prevents future segments from forming (any valid segmentation can be transformed into the greedy one without increasing the count). So scan once, accumulate GCD of the current segment, and cut immediately before an element that drops it to 1.
s: Start one segment with g = nums[0], answer = 1.
For each next element, g = gcd(g, x).
If g == 1, increment the answer and restart the segment with g = x.
a.t: O(n log V) — one GCD computation per element

w: Lead with the greedy — it is optimal and trivially fast; the DP is a safe fallback if you doubt the exchange argument. Note every single element has GCD equal to itself ≥ 2, so a solution always exists. Edge cases: a single element returns 1; coprime neighbors force cuts between them. Follow-up: what if subarrays were replaced by subsequences? Then the answer relates to distinct prime coverage and changes completely.
